newsitem.title: UK: N.Ireland in dark over Drumcree march decision.
newsitem.headline: N.Ireland in dark over Drumcree march decision.

text.p: Northern Ireland waited on Sunday for a decision whether the Orange Order will be allowed to hold parade that has become a set piece struggle between Protestant and Catholic communities.
Neither the Orangemen nor the Catholics of Portadown knows whether the authorities will ban, permit or re-route a march that is scheduled to start at 1000 (0900 GMT) from the centre of town.

British forces stepped up security during the night around the Drumcree church, from which the marchers' return with banners and bands would take them through an area where Catholic residents resent the parade as an annual reminder of Protestant dominance in the province's political life.
Witnesses saw troops stretch barbed wire across a narrow lane which would be part of the marchers' route and through nearby fields.

There was no official word from police chiefs or the British government over what decision would be made after the lengthy behind-the-scenes negotiations to defuse weeks of stand-off and rising tension in Portadown and across the province.

Dozens more Protestant parades are to be staged this week in the build-up to the 12th of July, the most cherished date in the Orange calendar which marks a 17th century Protestant victory over Britain's last Catholic king.

Orange Order officials say a decision to ban or re-route the parade would be a betrayal of their British loyalty and a surrender to Catholic Irish nationalists who see Dublin, not London, as their capital.

Portadown residents said they expect an announcement to be made shortly before the parade is due to start in an attempt to head off any move by militants of either side to oppose whatever decision is made.

British troops and local police in armoured cars and jeeps encircled the town and roads leading to the Garvaghy Road area, a Catholic enclave whose residents say the parade is sectarian intimidation and should be banned.
The planned route would take several hundred local Orange Order members from the town to an Anglican church at Drumcree for prayers and the back to town along the Garvaghy road.

Garvaghy road residents camped out on the pavements under Irish tricolour flags to claim the area as their own while the town's mainly Protestant people gathered under British Union Jack flags to speculate what the authorities would announce.

The Orange Order, named after the Protestant monarch William of Orange, says their ancestors have staged similar celebrations of their religion and British allegiance for decades and should not be prevented from what they intend as a peaceful demonstration.

Last year police did ban the parade but after almost five days of Protestant rioting they reversed their decision and hurried it through Garvaghy Road, igniting a wave of Catholic fury instead which blazed for several more days.

This year's planned march has confronted Britain's new Labour government with its first major political test of pledges to give equal rights to the pro-British Protestant majority and pro-Irish Catholic minority.

It has also clouded the backdrop to Anglo-Irish attempts to breathe new life into a Northern Ireland peace process which has been brought to its knees by guerrilla violence and mistrust by political leaders of both communities.
Britain has offered Sinn Fein, political wing of the Irish Republican Army (IRA), a place at peace talks if the IRA calls an end to its war against British rule of the province.
But officials of the two governments say they do not expect the IRA to show its hand until the so-called marching season is over.
Sinn Fein has challenged Britain to prove its commitment to respecting civil rights by stopping the Portadown parade.
